opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the RSA comparison is useful precisely because it's a case where checking is easy even though finding is hard. If someone hands you a factorization of a big number, you just multiply the factors together and see if you get the number back. There's a short, clean certificate, and verifying it is trivial. That's the dream situation for oversight: the system does something hard, and we can cheaply confirm it did it right.

The worry with neural networks is that most of the behaviors we care about don't come with that kind of certificate. Suppose a model is taking some action in a complicated environment, writing a big chunk of code, or giving advice about a policy decision. The question "was this good?" or "is this subtly sabotaged?" doesn't reduce to multiplying two numbers. The consequences might play out over a long time, depend on facts about the world we don't have access to, or depend on reasoning the model did internally that we can't see. So the gap between generating and verifying, which in RSA is in our favor, can actually be in the model's favor.

And there's an adversarial piece. With RSA, the math doesn't care whether the person handing you the factors wants to fool you; the check is airtight. With a neural network, if the model's objectives aren't what we intended, it's optimizing against whatever check we're running. Any blind spot in our evaluation becomes a place where bad behavior can hide. You could imagine a model that behaves perfectly on every input we test and then does something very different on some rare input, a trigger it recognizes, a situation where it thinks it won't be caught. Finding that input might be as hard as finding a needle in an exponentially large haystack.

That's a big part of why I care about things like interpretability and heuristic explanations. The hope is that even if we can't check the output directly, we can get some handle on *why* the model produced it, some structural account of the computation that would tell us "this behavior is coming from the same mechanism that worked fine on the training distribution" versus "something unusual is happening here." That would be a substitute for the clean certificate RSA gives you for free. But we don't really have that yet, and I think it's one of the central open problems.

r001.rationale: It contrasts RSA’s trivial factor check with neural network behaviors that lack clean certificates and can depend on long-term consequences or inaccessible reasoning, making them much harder to verify.

r002.rationale: It says a model could behave perfectly on every tested input yet act differently on a rare trigger, so passing easy tests does not establish that it succeeded on a difficult input.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the thing about RSA is that it was designed by humans who understood what they were doing, and so there's a story you can tell about why it works. If you want to know whether a given RSA implementation does the right thing, there's a mathematical argument, there's a spec, and the question of correctness decomposes into pieces that each have a reason behind them. Someone wrote the code with the intention that each line does a particular thing, and you can check that intention line by line.

A neural network isn't like that. Nobody designed it. There's no reason it's doing what it's doing other than that gradient descent found some set of weights that happen to produce good behavior on the training distribution. So when you hand it an input where you can't just look at the output and see if it's right, and you ask "did it do the right thing here?", you don't have anything to go on. There's no spec to compare against, and there's no human intention embedded in the weights that you could try to recover.

I think the deeper point is that for RSA, the reasons for its behavior are legible, and legible reasons are what let you verify behavior on inputs you haven't tested. For a neural network, the reasons exist, in some sense, the network is doing something for some reason, but they're not organized in a way that humans can understand or that any known tool can extract. And that's exactly the hard case. The easy inputs are the ones where you can check the answer directly. The difficult inputs are the ones where you'd need the reasons, and the reasons are the thing you don't have.

That's a lot of why I care about this. If we eventually have systems that are much more capable than us, almost all the inputs that matter are going to be difficult inputs in this sense, and "just check the output" stops being an option. So you'd either need some way to actually understand why the model is doing what it does, or some way to train it such that it's doing things for reasons you can supervise, and right now we don't really have either.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts RSA’s checkable mathematical reasons and line-by-line verification with having no usable basis to check a neural network on difficult inputs, conveying substantially greater verification difficulty.

r002.rationale: It says easy inputs can be checked directly, while difficult inputs require reasons that are unavailable, so checking easy cases does not establish whether the network is right on a hard input.

astra-6.text:
With RSA, you have a precise specification of what the algorithm is supposed to do. Even if the computation involves enormous numbers, you can check that each step follows the rules, and you can reason about why those rules give you the right result.

With a neural network, you can check that you multiplied the matrices correctly. But that’s not the thing you care about. You care whether the answer is true, or whether the action it’s taking is good. And on a difficult input, answering that question might require doing the same intellectual work you wanted the model to do in the first place.

So if I ask a model to evaluate a complicated scientific argument, it can give me something that looks convincing, but checking it may require expertise I don’t have. The difficulty isn’t verifying that the network executed correctly. It’s connecting that execution to the behavior we actually wanted.

r001.rationale: It contrasts checking RSA steps against judging whether a neural network’s answer is true or its action is good, noting that this may require the same intellectual work as the model and expertise the checker lacks.

r002.rationale: It discusses difficulty checking a hard input, but does not say that success on easy inputs may leave no way to tell whether the network fails on a hard one.

sol-6.1.text:
With RSA, you have a precise mathematical specification of what the algorithm is supposed to do. Even if the computation is complicated, you can check whether the output satisfies that specification. And you can potentially prove that the implementation does the right thing across all inputs.

With a neural network, the thing you want is often much harder to specify. Suppose you ask it for advice about some complicated situation. Checking whether that advice is actually good, or whether it’s misleading you in some subtle way, might require understanding the situation as well as the model does. There isn’t necessarily some short calculation you can do to check the answer.

So the difficulty isn’t just that the network is a complicated program. It’s that our criterion for correct behavior involves judgments that can themselves be very difficult. If the model is doing something beyond our ability to understand, then inspecting its behavior on a particular input may leave us with essentially the original hard problem.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts RSA’s precise, checkable specification with the difficulty of judging neural-network advice, which may require understanding the situation as well as the model and leave the original hard problem. This communicates that checking a difficult case can cost much more.

r002.rationale: The response discusses the difficulty of checking a hard input, but does not say that checking easy inputs may fail to reveal whether the network fails on a hard input.
